_note: Passages are stored with each question so questions can be shuffled independently. Repeat the passage text for every question that uses it.

questions.passage: In the early days of commercial aviation, the captain's authority in the cockpit was rarely questioned. Investigations of several accidents in the 1970s, however, found that other crew members had noticed problems but hesitated to speak up. In response, airlines developed training known as Crew Resource Management (CRM), which teaches every crew member to share observations, state concerns clearly, and work through decisions together. The captain still has final authority, but CRM treats the cockpit as a team in which good information can come from anyone. Today the approach has spread beyond aviation to fields such as surgery and firefighting.
questions.prompt: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
choices: Captains no longer have authority in the cockpit.
CRM was developed to improve communication and teamwork among flight crews.
Most accidents in the 1970s were caused by mechanical failure.
CRM was first developed for surgeons and firefighters.
Airline training has become shorter over time.
questions.explanation: The passage explains why CRM was created and what it teaches. Choice A contradicts the passage, which says the captain keeps final authority.

questions.passage: Pilots often say that hot, high, and humid conditions are an airplane's enemy. As air warms, rises in elevation, or holds more moisture, it becomes less dense. Thinner air gives the wings less to push against, so the airplane needs a longer runway to reach takeoff speed, and the engine and propeller produce less power. The combined effect is described as density altitude: the altitude at which the airplane performs as though it were operating. On a summer afternoon at a mountain airport, density altitude can be thousands of feet higher than the field's actual elevation, and a takeoff that is routine on a cool morning may become dangerous.
questions.prompt: Based on the passage, which conditions would most likely INCREASE the takeoff distance an airplane needs?
choices: Cold, dry air at a sea-level airport
A cool morning at a mountain airport
A longer runway
Dense air over the ocean
A hot, humid afternoon at a high-elevation airport
questions.explanation: Heat, elevation, and humidity all thin the air, which lengthens the takeoff run. Choice E combines all three.

choices: the actual elevation of the airport

questions.explanation: The passage defines it as the altitude at which the airplane performs as though it were operating, which can differ from the real field elevation.
